transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-08-15
Start time: 14:00 PDT
Duration: 45 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Mia Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Ruiz (Redwood SE), John Park (Acme Eng Mgr), Priya Desai (Acme SRE), Evan Lee (Acme Security)

Summary (auto): Quick console walkthrough focused on tracing and request logs. Discussed debugging flow from traces to request logs, query examples, export options, and security concerns (KMS, SOC2). Next steps: docs and pilot plan.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Mia Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Can you all hear me okay?
[00:06] John Park: Yep, loud and clear. Thanks Mia.
[00:08] Priya: Hi, yes, thanks. We got your invite.
[00:10] Carlos Ruiz: Great, hi team. I'm Carlos, I'm the solutions engineer. Mia and I will run through the console tracing + request logs flow and then we can dig into the pilot.
[00:20] John Park: High level, we're most interested in debugging production errors for our transaction pipeline  latency spikes and malformed model outputs.
[00:28] Mia Chen: Perfect, that'll be the focus. Quick agenda: tracing overview, error analysis demo, request log fields and exports, then pilot logistics. Any other must-cover items?
[00:36] Evan Lee: I want to confirm encryption at rest and KMS integration, plus audit logs retention.
[00:42] Mia Chen: We'll cover that briefly and follow up with SOC2 artifacts.

[00:50] Carlos Ruiz: Ok jumping into the console  bear with me, I'm sharing my screen. So on the left is the Tracing tab. We model requests as a parent span per API call and child spans for key steps: tokenization, model inference, retries, network.
[01:10] Carlos Ruiz: Here's a sample trace for a failed transaction request  you can see a long tail on the model inference span, and an error tag on the business logic step.
[01:22] Priya: The timestamps in those spans, are they in UTC?
[01:25] Carlos Ruiz: Yes, stored in UTC; UI shows local by default.
[01:30] John Park: Can we search traces by customer_id + model_version? That's important for us.
[01:36] Carlos Ruiz: Yes, you can filter by multiple attributes  we index common fields like request_id, customer_id, model_version, route. For ad-hoc fields, you can use tag search.
[01:48] Mia Chen: Also note we automatically link traces to request logs when available  so clicking a trace takes you to the raw request payload and response.

[02:05] Speaker 1 (John): That's useful  if we see a malformed output we want to pull the exact prompt and model config used.
[02:12] Carlos Ruiz: Exactly. Here's the request logs view  each row is an API call with key columns: timestamp, request_id, customer_id, route, model_version, latency_ms, status_code. You can click into a row to see full request and response JSON including headers and token counts.
[02:28] Priya: What's the default retention on request logs?
[02:31] Carlos Ruiz: Default is 30 days for hosted, configurable for Dedicated/Private but the UI will show your plan's retention. Exports to S3 or streamed to our partner SIEMs are supported.
[02:43] Evan Lee: For Private, can logs be kept in our S3 only? We need to ensure we don't leave copies behind.
[02:49] Mia Chen: For Private deployments you can configure local retention and S3 buckets under customer control; we support customer-managed KMS and can disable secondary copies. We'll share the deployment checklist.

[03:05] Carlos Ruiz: Back to the trace, if you expand the inference span you can see sub-steps  compilation, kernel selection, kv-cache hit/miss. That KV hit/miss tag is useful for diagnosing throughput regressions.
[03:20] John Park: Nice. Can we set alerts off traces where latency > 500ms for inference span?
[03:27] Carlos Ruiz: Yes  you can create an alert rule in the Console that triggers on span latency percentiles or on aggregate metrics for a route or customer_id. We can show an example alert in the next session.

[03:40] Mia Chen: Quick live demo: I'm going to simulate an error by replaying a failed request from our logs.
[03:48] [04:00] Carlos Ruiz: (replaying) Ok I triggered the same trace. You can see the error tag message says "invalid prompt tokens"  notice the request body here has an unexpected control char from the upstream parser.
[04:14] John Park: That's exactly like the bug we saw last week. If we have the trace linked to request log we can triage faster.
[04:21] Priya: Do you keep the model's raw logits or only final text? We sometimes need logits to debug hallucinations.
[04:28] Carlos Ruiz: By default we store inputs and outputs; storing logits is opt-in on Dedicated/Private because of cost and size  we can enable it for the pilot if you want.
[04:37] Evan Lee: Opt-in is fine but need a data retention policy. We'll need a policy for PII redaction too.
[04:44] Mia Chen: Totally  we have built-in PII redaction, and you can annotate fields to be redacted before storage. We'll include that in the SOC2 docs.

[05:00] [05:30] Carlos Ruiz: Now the error analysis tab  this aggregates recent errors by route, model_version, and error class. You can open an error group and see sample traces and request logs side-by-side.
[05:45] Carlos Ruiz: For example here's a spike in "timeout" errors last Thursday, the UI shows top contributing routes and a timeline. You can jump from that view into query builder to filter by timeframe and customer.
[06:00] Priya: Can we export those error groups into a CSV or ticketing tool?
[06:05] Carlos Ruiz: Yes, export to CSV and we have integrations for Jira/ServiceNow to create incidents with attached traces.

[06:18] John Park: About data residency  we process most traffic in us-west but we need EU region for EU customers. Do you have region-specific log routing?
[06:26] Mia Chen: Yes, you can pin routes to regions; for Hosted we have EU regions with separate retention. For Dedicated we can provision capacity in the region you need.

[06:40] [07:00] Carlos Ruiz: Quick aside on performance, the console also surfaces per-model token throughput and average kv-cache hit rate per route  that helps pick optimization levers.
[07:12] John Park: That kv cache metric  is it per customer or global?
[07:15] Carlos Ruiz: Per route by default, and you can slice by customer_id. It's computed from aggregated requests over the configured window.

[07:30] Priya: For the pilot, we want to run 3 tests: 1) error reproduction using sample malformed inputs, 2) latency stress test with sustained QPS ~200, 3) trace-based regression for model version rollout. Will Redwood be able to ingest our test traffic?
[07:48] Carlos Ruiz: Yes  we'll provide a test harness or you can replay anonymized traffic via our ingestion API. We'll give you a template for event format.

[08:02] Mia Chen: Let's demo a debugging flow: say a user files a ticket that an invoice generation returned wrong amounts. You search by customer_id and time window, find traces with high inference latency and an error span on the business logic. Click through to request logs, inspect the prompt and model_version, then you can re-run the request in the sandbox to confirm.
[08:26] John Park: Re-run in sandbox  does that use the same model weights? We don't want to affect production state.
[08:32] Carlos Ruiz: The sandbox clones the same model version for inference-only replay; it doesn't change production state. It's a safe replay.

[08:45] Evan Lee: Regarding RBAC  can we limit who can view raw request payloads?
[08:50] Mia Chen: Yes  RBAC is role-based, you can create a role that has trace/metrics view but not request_payload_view. We'll share the mapping and examples.
[09:00] Priya: How are audit logs surfaced? We need to show who accessed which requests for compliance.
[09:06] Carlos Ruiz: All UI and API accesses are logged to the audit stream; you can export to your SIEM or view in the Console with filters for actor and resource.

[09:20] [10:00] Carlos Ruiz: Now a couple of quick queries  in the request logs search you can run an ad-hoc SQL-like query. For example: SELECT count(*) FROM requests WHERE model_version='v2.1' AND status_code!=200 GROUP BY error_class.
[10:22] John Park: Is that query runtime heavy? Could it affect production?
[10:26] Carlos Ruiz: Queries run against an analytics store and are rate-limited; they don't hit the production serving tier. For heavy queries we recommend exports to your BI tool.

[10:40] Mia Chen: Time check  we're about 30 minutes in. Want to spend the last part on pilot scope and timelines.
[10:48] John Park: Sounds good. For success criteria we need: reduce mean time to resolution (MTTR) for transaction errors to <30 minutes, and detect model-output regressions before they reach 1% error-rate in production.
[10:59] Priya: Also need encryption keys managed by us (BYOK), and log retention policy of at least 90 days for some EU customers.

[11:12] Carlos Ruiz: For BYOK we support customer-managed KMS for Private and Dedicated; for Hosted we have a KMS integration option. Retention for Dedicated/Private can be configured to 90+ days.
[11:24] Mia Chen: Next steps then: I'll send SOC2 and deployment checklist, Carlos will draft pilot plan and test templates, John to share sample traffic profile and SLOs. We'll aim to kick off pilot the week of 2026-08-24.

[11:40] Evan Lee: One last question  any known limitations around streaming responses and tracing correlation? We use streaming for invoice generation.
[11:48] Carlos Ruiz: Streaming responses have per-chunk spans but we correlate them under the same request_id; there's a small caveat for out-of-order chunk arrival in some network paths, but we annotate those events in the trace.
[12:02] John Park: Cool. This was helpful.
[12:05] Mia Chen: Great  thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the documents and the pilot checklist.
[12:10] Priya: Thanks folks.
[12:12] Carlos Ruiz: Thanks, bye.

--- End transcript ---

Notes: occasional ASR artifacts  speaker labels may be approximate. References to "kv-cache" and "kernel selection" correspond to Redwood runtime internals. Links shared during call: SOC2 pack (link: https://redwood.ai/soc2), pilot template (link: https://redwood.ai/pilot-template), RBAC docs (link: https://redwood.ai/rbac).
